headline: Carbon Credits Give Millions of Africans Access to Clean Cooking

summary_short: Carbon credits are making clean cookstoves affordable across Africa, with $900 million in new financing helping millions of low-income households transition away from ch…
body:
Across Africa, carbon credit financing is quietly transforming how millions of low-income households cook their meals. Companies like Kenya's BURN are using carbon credits to subsidize the cost of electric and efficient biomass cookstoves, making clean cooking accessible to families who might otherwise rely on charcoal stoves and open fires. With governments introducing supportive policies and securing $900 million in fresh financing commitments, the approach addresses three urgent challenges at once: it expands access to cleaner cooking methods, helps reduce the continent's deforestation crisis, and cuts the hazardous household air pollution that affects countless families daily.

The mechanics are straightforward. Carbon credits—financial instruments that represent emissions reductions—provide the funding needed to lower stove prices for consumers who cannot afford them upfront. As cleaner cookstoves replace traditional charcoal fires, the resulting emissions reductions generate additional carbon credits, creating a cycle that funds further expansion. In Kiambu, Kenya, families like Mary Kavutha's are already using fuel-efficient BURN stoves to prepare their daily meals, embodying this shift in real households across the region.

Yet the promise of this approach hinges on a single critical factor: sustained demand for high-integrity carbon credits in global markets. If that demand weakens, the financing that makes clean stoves affordable could dry up, threatening the momentum of Africa's clean cooking transition. For now, though, carbon credits represent an innovative pathway—one that doesn't ask Africa's poorest households to bear the full cost of the clean energy future.
